title: Jensen Huang's return ignites violent rally, but every problem remains unresolved
dek: Barclays strategist says this rally is not a fundamental reversal, but short covering and low liquidity working together; AI funding and revenue structural problems haven't moved one bit since yesterday.
why: Rare real-time record of how markets jumped from ‘AI bubble bursting’ to ‘epic rally’ in 72 hours; strategist provides technical explanations but admits fundamental problems stay unresolved; for investors seeking to understand this violent swing's mechanics, not headlines.
who: Investors and traders tracking US equity volatility mechanics, AI compute infrastructure funding risks, and the politicization of Nvidia governance.

points.h: It's not a dead cat bounce, the volatility mechanism changed
points.body: When asked if this is a dead cat bounce, Altman says no—but not because fundamentals improved. VIX fell from Friday's 40 to 30, which still means normal daily moves near 2%. The S&P fell roughly 7% last week, the worst week since COVID, so large swings both ways should be normal expectations, not anomalies. This reframes whether the bounce is credible as a pure volatility mechanics question, not a narrative one.

points.h: Friday's selloff looked exactly like the COVID moment
points.body: Altman describes Friday's last two hours of S&P volatility as strikingly similar to COVID's pattern. Behind it: roughly $35 billion in leveraged ETF selling, plus Thursday being the 58th worst trading day for liquidity in the past decade. Dealers held short gamma positions near S&P 7100; when the index broke that level, it triggered more delta selling, a negative feedback loop. This, not fundamental panic, is the true mechanism of Friday's crash.

points.h: Jensen Huang's return cannot answer any real questions
points.body: Altman is direct: in August, their case for being bearish on AI had two parts—how will funding materialize, and can revenue track the trajectory after so much capital deployed so quickly. Those questions had no answers then and have no answers now. Jensen's return changes nothing here. The quantitative model has turned to bullish signals, worthy of tactical buying, but that's just a technical judgment that risk asymmetry has shifted. The fundamental questions haven't budged.

points.h: Trump administration stepped in to prop markets, complicating traders' bets
points.body: On whether the White House is backstopping Jensen and AI trades, Altman compares this kind of political volatility to tariffs: sentiment can flip ‘on a dime or a tweet or a Truth Social post’. Making year-end bets on a fragile narrative is tricky. But the data tells a story: 35% of US household net wealth is stocks, two-thirds of households own stocks—the highest equity exposure for households since the late 1920s. That explains why the government has strong motive to prop this up.

points.h: Fed December rate hike is priced in, but language carries the risk
points.body: The market's sensitivity isn't about whether the Fed hikes in December—that's priced in. The risk is whether Fed language reveals ‘obliviousness’ to the broader funding environment. Altman points to datacenter bonds like Coreweave, whose spreads haven't tightened; SpaceX's recent bond issuance proves higher financing costs are real. This thread runs straight back to whether AI buildout can keep accessing capital.

points.h: Having the 2018 tightening warning's author repeat the mistake: ironic
points.body: Altman draws a parallel to December 2018, when Druckenmiller and Kevin Walsh co-authored a warning against excess tightening. The irony: if the FOMC ignores market internals and tightens anyway, the person who warned about that mistake could be repeating it. If the Fed is completely out of sync with market signals, then this bounce truly is a dead cat bounce.

points.h: Semiconductor stocks' crash is itself the most important new data point
points.body: Asked whether the past three weeks brought new data bolstering or undermining overbuild fears, Altman's answer is: price is data. Semiconductors fell 30% to 40%; SK Hynix trades at an extremely compressed forward P/E. This deleveraging cleared out bad sentiment—positions like 3x longs on Hynix, 3x shorts on Nvidia. Bad assets leaving the system itself supports the bounce, even if the valuation floor could go lower.

points.h: Trump's deep governance involvement leaves behind political land mines
points.body: Here's a new tension: Washington is explicitly backing Jensen and Nvidia's recovery. Normally you don't want to oppose the Fed or the government. But many view Trump as a lame duck. His deep involvement in a major US company's governance becomes a glaring target for Democratic investigation—especially if Democrats take the White House in 2028. This political risk remains completely unresolved.
